title: Protocol for Diabetes Mellitus Type I or Type II Insulin Treated - CGM Option

blocks.text: Consideration will be given to those individuals who have been clinically stable on their current treatment regimen for a period of 6-months or more. The FAA has an established policy that permits the special issuance medical certification to some insulin treated applicants. Individuals certificated under this policy will be required to provide medical documentation regarding their history of treatment, accidents, and current medical status. If certificated, they will be required to adhere to monitoring requirements. There are no restrictions regarding flight outside of the United States air space. Airmen with a current 3rd class certificate will have the limitation removed with their next certificate. If they need the limitation removed sooner, they should contact AMCD for an updated certificate without the limitation.

  • 2. Analyze to identify percentage time in the following ranges:

        • a) Less than 54 mg/dL
        • b) Less than 70mg/dL
        • c) Between 70 and 180 mg/dL
        • d) Above 180 mg/dL
        • e) Above 250 mg/dL

blocks.text: - B. CGM DEVICE FEATURES: The FAA does not endorse any particular manufacturer, however, the CGM device must have the following features:
blocks.html: • B. CGM DEVICE FEATURES: The FAA does not endorse any particular manufacturer, however, the CGM device must have the following features:

• 1. Must be FDA-approved and appropriate for age;
  • 2. Must be a real-time CGM (automatically transmits glucose data to the user) without need to manually scan the sensor (e.g., intermittently scanned CGM);
  • 3. Have “predictive arrow trends” that provide warnings of potentially dangerous glucose levels (high or low) before they occur;
  • 4. Able to customize low and high glucose levels;
  • 5. Have a high-accuracy rating with an overall Mean Absolute Relative Difference (MARD) of 10% or less. (e.g., If the MARD is 10% and the glucose reading is 70mg/dL, the actual blood glucose could be as low as 63 mg/dL or as high as 77mg/dL);
  • 6. Printout reports must include monthly summary showing: Time-In-Range (TIR) Values for 70- 180 mg/dL; Average Glucose Levels; Standard Deviation (SD); and (when provided by the reporting software) Coefficient of Variability [CoV] values. Reports must include weekly glucose value data graphics. All data must be legible. Failure to provide these values could result in a delay in processing your application;
  • 7. Calibrated to at least at the minimum frequency required by the manufacturer or endocrinologist; and

  • 8. Must be individual’s own, unblinded CGM that cannot be shared with anyone else. The individual cannot use anyone else’s CGM (e.g., blinded CGM device, which is professional use only).

blocks.text: POLICY FAQs
blocks.html: POLICY FAQs

blocks.text: - 1. What did it take to develop an insulin-use policy for Class I and II medical certificate for the FAA?
blocks.html: • 1. What did it take to develop an insulin-use policy for Class I and II medical certificate for the FAA?

blocks.text: Advances in diabetes management utilizing CGM technology provides pilots and the FAA better information about blood glucose levels and advanced warning of potentially dangerous glucose levels before they occur. CGM technology also allows the FAA to evaluate consistency of blood glucose control both in flight and on the ground.
blocks.html: Advances in diabetes management utilizing CGM technology provides pilots and the FAA better information about blood glucose levels and advanced warning of potentially dangerous glucose levels before they occur. CGM technology also allows the FAA to evaluate consistency of blood glucose control both in flight and on the ground.

blocks.text: - 2. Why did the FAA take so long to develop an insulin-use policy for Class I/II airmen especially when other countries have allowed it for years?
blocks.html: • 2. Why did the FAA take so long to develop an insulin-use policy for Class I/II airmen especially when other countries have allowed it for years?

blocks.text: Various flight safety considerations for this serious health condition could not be safely mitigated for commercial operations until recently. Advances in technology and diabetes management now provide the FAA better parameters to consider Class I and II medical certification for some insulin-dependent airmen.
blocks.html: Various flight safety considerations for this serious health condition could not be safely mitigated for commercial operations until recently. Advances in technology and diabetes management now provide the FAA better parameters to consider Class I and II medical certification for some insulin-dependent airmen.

blocks.text: At the time of initial publication, only Canada and the United Kingdom allow the use of insulin in their pilots with an equivalent Class I or II medical. Unlike the FAA, those aviation authorities can impose specific operational limitations on the medical certificate (e.g., “valid only for two pilot operations” or requiring the other pilot to be both aware of the diabetic condition and able to provide emergency treatment.)
blocks.html: At the time of initial publication, only Canada and the United Kingdom allow the use of insulin in their pilots with an equivalent Class I or II medical. Unlike the FAA, those aviation authorities can impose specific operational limitations on the medical certificate (e.g., “valid only for two pilot operations” or requiring the other pilot to be both aware of the diabetic condition and able to provide emergency treatment.)

blocks.text: - 3. Why is the FAA so restrictive and why is there so much testing?
blocks.html: • 3. Why is the FAA so restrictive and why is there so much testing?

blocks.text: The FAA policy follows current medical standards of care for diabetes to ensure pilots are safe to fly in the complex aviation environment and reduce the risks of end-organ damage. If the latter is present, the potential risk of cognitive impairment is increased, which could be magnified in a hypoxic or high-stress environment, affecting safety.
blocks.html: The FAA policy follows current medical standards of care for diabetes to ensure pilots are safe to fly in the complex aviation environment and reduce the risks of end-organ damage. If the latter is present, the potential risk of cognitive impairment is increased, which could be magnified in a hypoxic or high-stress environment, affecting safety.

blocks.text: - 4. My doctor says my diabetes is well controlled and that I have no limitations. Why doesn’t FAA accept that?
blocks.html: • 4. My doctor says my diabetes is well controlled and that I have no limitations. Why doesn’t FAA accept that?

blocks.text: While your physicians understand how to keep your blood sugar stable while on the ground, they may not be familiar with the additional challenges of the demanding aviation environment and may not consider them when determining clinical limitations. FAA guidance addresses these aviation-specific concerns.
blocks.html: While your physicians understand how to keep your blood sugar stable while on the ground, they may not be familiar with the additional challenges of the demanding aviation environment and may not consider them when determining clinical limitations. FAA guidance addresses these aviation-specific concerns.

blocks.text: - 5. Are there additional risks when flying with diabetes?
blocks.html: • 5. Are there additional risks when flying with diabetes?

blocks.text: Yes. Hypoglycemia can lead to cognitive impairment, loss of consciousness, and seizure. Hyperglycemia can potentially cause sudden incapacitation, but it can also cause damage to eyes, heart, kidneys, and nervous system.

blocks.text: BLOOD SUGAR FAQs
blocks.html: BLOOD SUGAR FAQs

blocks.text: - 6. Why is the blood sugar range so narrow?
blocks.html: • 6. Why is the blood sugar range so narrow?

blocks.text: The recommended blood glucose range is not intended to be “narrow,” but reflects generally accepted treatment guidelines and the needs of safety. Safety concerns arise when blood sugar falls outside of the 70mg/dl - 250 mg/dL range.
blocks.html: The recommended blood glucose range is not intended to be “narrow,” but reflects generally accepted treatment guidelines and the needs of safety. Safety concerns arise when blood sugar falls outside of the 70mg/dl - 250 mg/dL range.

blocks.text: - 7. Why do I need to use a CGM device even when I’m not flying? I am well controlled with finger sticks and injections. Why do I need to follow these new rules?
blocks.html: • 7. Why do I need to use a CGM device even when I’m not flying? I am well controlled with finger sticks and injections. Why do I need to follow these new rules?

blocks.text: CGM technology allows the FAA to ensure ongoing safety through consistent blood glucose control both in flight and on the ground regardless of the pilot’s flight schedule.
blocks.html: CGM technology allows the FAA to ensure ongoing safety through consistent blood glucose control both in flight and on the ground regardless of the pilot’s flight schedule.

blocks.text: - 8. I am currently on a Special Issuance (SI) for another condition. How will ITDM affect that?
blocks.html: • 8. I am currently on a Special Issuance (SI) for another condition. How will ITDM affect that?

blocks.text: Your existing SI will be invalid due to the additional diagnosis. You will need a new authorization letter.
blocks.html: Your existing SI will be invalid due to the additional diagnosis. You will need a new authorization letter.

blocks.text: - 9. What do I do if I develop symptoms or become incapacitated/impaired due to my blood glucose levels while I am on a trip?
blocks.html: • 9. What do I do if I develop symptoms or become incapacitated/impaired due to my blood glucose levels while I am on a trip?

• You must disqualify yourself from flight activities as required by both the SI and 14 CFR 61.53;
  • Contact your treating endocrinologist to determine if there is a need to change your insulin treatment; and

  • • Contact your AME with details surrounding the event.

    • Your AME should contact the FAA to discuss your case.

blocks.text: CONTINUOUS GLUCOSE MONITOR (CGM) AND INSULIN PUMP FAQs
blocks.html: CONTINUOUS GLUCOSE MONITOR (CGM) AND INSULIN PUMP FAQs

blocks.text: - 10. Which CGMs does the FAA allow?
blocks.html: • 10. Which CGMs does the FAA allow?

blocks.text: The FAA lists the required functions of CGMs in the Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners (AME Guide). While we do not endorse specific brands, we have added a list of devices we know meet these requirements. See “Item # 4 - Continuous Glucose Monitor Data” of the ITDM Initial Certificate Consideration Requirements .

While we do not endorse specific brands, we have added a list of devices we know meet these requirements. See “Item # 4 - Continuous Glucose Monitor Data” of the ITDM Initial Certificate Consideration Requirements .

blocks.text: - 11. Why is a CGM required instead of finger stick blood sugar?
blocks.html: • 11. Why is a CGM required instead of finger stick blood sugar?

blocks.text: The CGM is more accurate, measuring within 10% of the actual blood sugar. It is also independent of the pilot’s action. Turbulence can make it impossible for pilots to perform finger sticks, even with an autopilot and/or second pilot. The CGMs can enable notifications and alerts for specific blood glucose values and show predictive trends, both of which are required. The CGM can also communicate with an insulin pump.

blocks.text: - 12. How do I know if my CGM and/or insulin pump is legal for flight as an “authorized personal electronic device?”
blocks.html: • 12. How do I know if my CGM and/or insulin pump is legal for flight as an “authorized personal electronic device?”

blocks.text: Most current medical devices should be approved; however, the pilot needs to verify this with the aircraft operator for the aircraft that they fly. It is not feasible for the FAA to maintain a list of approved devices due to the rapidly changing technology and to the large number of airframe and avionics combinations seen in the Part 91, 91k, 121, and 135 fleets.

It is not feasible for the FAA to maintain a list of approved devices due to the rapidly changing technology and to the large number of airframe and avionics combinations seen in the Part 91, 91k, 121, and 135 fleets.

blocks.text: See AC 20-164A for guidance.

blocks.text: - 13. I know I have to submit CGM data to the FAA. How do I get this information?
blocks.html: • 13. I know I have to submit CGM data to the FAA. How do I get this information?

blocks.text: Most devices have the ability to print out customized data reports to your computer. Check your device’s user guide for instructions as well as computer and software requirements as these may differ between manufacturers. (Note: Some devices will not allow the export of data onto your phone or tablet.)

Check your device’s user guide for instructions as well as computer and software requirements as these may differ between manufacturers. blocks.text: - 14. What do I do if my CGM device fails?
blocks.html: • 14. What do I do if my CGM device fails?

blocks.text: You should have all the following available during flight:
blocks.html: You should have all the following available during flight:

blocks.text:
- Glucometer (glucose meter) and test strips.
- Backup sensor for the CGM device.
- Backup insulin pen available if using an insulin pump.
blocks.html:
• Glucometer (glucose meter) and test strips.
  • Backup sensor for the CGM device.
  • Backup insulin pen available if using an insulin pump.

blocks.text: If the CGM stops working, go to a back-up plan for the remainder of the flight and measure your finger stick blood sugar every 30 minutes. If you are unable to correct your blood sugar, treat this as any in flight emergency and land as soon as practicable.
blocks.html: If the CGM stops working, go to a back-up plan for the remainder of the flight and measure your finger stick blood sugar every 30 minutes. If you are unable to correct your blood sugar, treat this as any in flight emergency and land as soon as practicable.

blocks.text: - 15. Do I have to get an insulin pump?
blocks.html: • 15. Do I have to get an insulin pump?

blocks.text: No. However, if you choose to get an insulin pump, both the pump and CGM need to be FDA approved, both separately and in combination. Self-built systems are NOT acceptable for flying.
blocks.html: No. However, if you choose to get an insulin pump, both the pump and CGM need to be FDA approved, both separately and in combination. Self-built systems are NOT acceptable for flying.

blocks.text: - 16. Are there any concerns with the insulin pumps?
blocks.html: • 16. Are there any concerns with the insulin pumps?

blocks.text: Yes, the pump could potentially fail or malfunction delivering too little or too much insulin.
blocks.html: Yes, the pump could potentially fail or malfunction delivering too little or too much insulin.

blocks.text:
- In the event of failure or malfunction, a backup insulin delivery must be available.
- In the event of sudden cabin depressurization, consider turning off or disconnecting the pump.
- If necessary, clear any bubbles in tubing seen with changes in cabin pressure.
blocks.html:
• In the event of failure or malfunction, a backup insulin delivery must be available.
  • In the event of sudden cabin depressurization, consider turning off or disconnecting the pump.
  • If necessary, clear any bubbles in tubing seen with changes in cabin pressure.

blocks.text: - 17. Are there any features that make some insulin pumps better for flying?
blocks.html: • 17. Are there any features that make some insulin pumps better for flying?

blocks.text: The ability to suspend insulin delivery for a low reading is a good safety feature. In addition, a pump in which the insulin reservoir is not in direct line for delivery is preferred.
blocks.html: The ability to suspend insulin delivery for a low reading is a good safety feature. In addition, a pump in which the insulin reservoir is not in direct line for delivery is preferred.

blocks.text: - 18. I do not use an insulin pump. Do I need to make any changes from my normal routine on the days that I fly?
blocks.html: • 18. I do not use an insulin pump. Do I need to make any changes from my normal routine on the days that I fly?

blocks.text: The goal is to avoid hypoglycemia while flying. Talk with your board-certified endocrinologist about whether or not adjustments should be made on days when you are flying.
blocks.html: The goal is to avoid hypoglycemia while flying. Talk with your board-certified endocrinologist about whether or not adjustments should be made on days when you are flying.

blocks.text: - 19. What do I do if my device breaks while traveling or I run out of supplies?
blocks.html: • 19. What do I do if my device breaks while traveling or I run out of supplies?

blocks.text:
- Replace the machine as soon as possible.
- If you cannot do this, finish the scheduled trip with your back-up system (finger sticks and injections) and remain compliant with the SI.
- Once the trip concludes, do not start a new trip until the system authorized in the SI is back in place and functional.
- While you may complete at trip once on the road, you are NOT authorized to add additional legs to the trip.
- If neither the primary nor the backup system is functional, you must terminate flight activity. This is an absolute flight safety requirement.
blocks.html:
• Replace the machine as soon as possible.
  • If you cannot do this, finish the scheduled trip with your back-up system (finger sticks and injections) and remain compliant with the SI.
  • Once the trip concludes, do not start a new trip until the system authorized in the SI is back in place and functional.
  • While you may complete at trip once on the road, you are NOT authorized to add additional legs to the trip.
  • If neither the primary nor the backup system is functional, you must terminate flight activity. This is an absolute flight safety requirement.

blocks.text: - 20. Is there a required ground time if I change pumps or CGM devices?
blocks.html: • 20. Is there a required ground time if I change pumps or CGM devices?

blocks.text:
- If you are already using a pump or CGM device and you change devices, no there is no ground time.
- If you have NEVER used a pump previously, and you start using a pump for the first time, there is a seven (7) day ground trial period.
- There is no required ground time if changing from an “open loop” to a “closed loop” system.

• If you are already using a pump or CGM device and you change devices, no there is no ground time.
  • If you have NEVER used a pump previously, and you start using a pump for the first time, there is a seven (7) day ground trial period.
  • There is no required ground time if changing from an “open loop” to a “closed loop” system.
